newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine peso woes not yet over-bankers.
newsitem.headline: Philippine peso woes not yet over-bankers.

text.p: The Philippines could still be forced into a drawn-out war to defend its currency after speculators pressured Thailand to change in exchange rate policy to a managed float, bankers said on Wednesday.
"I hope the speculators don't move to the Philippines and think the Philippines would have to bite the bullet as well," said Banco Santander treasurer Antonio Agcaoili.
"They're saying the local currency is likewise overvalued and therefore fundamentals don't support the peso-dollar level," he said.
Exporters have been urging the government to allow a weaker peso to make their products more competitive in the world market.
The Philippine Central Bank put up a strong defense of the peso after Thailand announced that it was allowing a managed float of its currency.
It raised its overnight borrowing rate by a total of nine percentage points on Wednesday to 24 percent and sold dollars heavily.
The peos closed at 26.376 from a previous 26.374. Speculation on the peso drove volume in the market to a record $1.05 billion.
Thailand's persistent financial woes have spilled over into the Philippines as investors drew comparisons with Thailand where an overheated property market affected its banking industry.
Finance Secretary Roberto de Ocampo said the Philippines won't be forced into the same situation as Thailand.
"Thailand tended to peg its currency. Ours is managed but market-oriented," he said.
"I do not believe the Philippines will be forced to a change in exchange rate policy," said Hongkong and Shanghai Bank treasurer Mark Boyne, adding the Philippines' economic fundamentals remain good.
But because of the spillover effect of Thai's change in policy, he said the Central Bank's key overnight borrowing rate is not likely to fall below 15 percent for the rest of the month.

"I think the problem had been more drawn-out than initially expected and therefore rates would have to stay higher than people expected," he said. "I think the Central Bank will adopt a cautious policy."
Speculators, however, may be discouraged from picking on the peso because of the absence of offshore spot trading unlike for the Thai baht, said Santander's Agcaoili.
"Speculators cannot really drive the peso down," Jaime Panganiban, treasurer of Bank of America, said.
He cited Bankers Association rules which impose a temporary halt in peso trading should it move more than 1 1/2 percent from its opening rate.
Documentation requirements by the Central Bank also make it difficult to buy large amounts of dollars, he added.
Though slightly higher interest rates and a weaker peso may come about from the recent developments, the impact would be short-lived, De Ocampo said.
"An IMF team is in town and they're about to leave here giving us a clean bill of health and a lot of strong statements that our economy is in good shape," he said.
-- Manila newsroom (63 2) 841-8937
